reason: The text does not depict Hebrew leaders being antagonistic to the Hebrew people. Rather, it shows: (1) Moses, an emerging Hebrew leader, going out to see his brethren and their burdens under Egyptian oppression, and striking an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew; (2) when Moses attempts to intervene in a dispute between two Hebrew men, one man challenges his authority, but this reflects internal Hebrew conflict rather than established leadership being antagonistic to the people; and (3) the clear antagonistic force in the passage is Pharaoh (Egyptian leadership) seeking to kill Moses. The passage emphasizes Hebrew suffering under Egyptian oppression, not Hebrew leaders being antagonistic to their own people.
